1.title: Cost-Optimized Network Architectures
1.text: Welcome to Module fourteen: Cost-Optimized Network Architectures. This module covers task statement four point four, the last content task of Domain four, Design Cost-Optimized Architectures. You will find where data transfer charges come from, choose N A T layouts and endpoints that cut cost, compare connection options, and use edge caching, routing and throttling to move fewer bytes. The exam describes a traffic path and asks you to remove its costliest hop.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Find where data transfer charges come from. Choose N A T gateway layouts and V P C endpoints that cut cost. Compare Direct Connect, V P N and the internet, and peering, Transit Gateway and Private Link. Use C D Ns, edge caching, routing and throttling to reduce transfer. And review existing workloads for network savings.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lantern and Loom Trims the Network Bill
1.text: The network bill at Lantern and Loom keeps rising. Three N A T gateways run in a test V P C. Private servers pull terabytes from S three through a N A T gateway. Overseas shoppers download images straight from the Region. And a steady, large data feed goes to the head office over the internet. Your job is to find the waste.

1.title: Where Network Cost Comes From
1.text: Learn the order of network cost. Data into A W S from the internet is free. Data out to the internet is charged per gigabyte. Data between Regions is charged per gigabyte. Data between Availability Zones in a Region is also charged per gigabyte, in both directions. Data in the same zone over a private I P address is free. Traffic through a N A T gateway is charged hourly, plus per gigabyte processed. And public I P version four addresses carry an hourly charge. Prefer private paths and same-zone traffic where the design allows. Exact rates change, so learn the order, not the numbers. Exam tip: data in is free; data out, across Regions and across zones costs money.

1.title: NAT Gateway Cost
1.text: A N A T gateway lets private subnets reach the internet. A N A T instance means you pay for an instance and manage it; it is cheap at tiny scale, with limited bandwidth, and it is a single point of failure. One shared N A T gateway has the lowest cost, with cross-zone traffic, and one zone as the failure point. One N A T gateway per zone costs more, is resilient, and avoids cross-zone N A T traffic. A regional N A T gateway is one I D that expands across zones, for a simpler design. A N A T gateway bills hourly plus per gigabyte processed. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, check regional N A T gateway pricing and Region availability. Exam tip: production needs a N A T gateway per zone for resilience; test and development can share one.

1.title: Avoiding NAT Cost with VPC Endpoints
1.text: The figure shows a private subnet with two paths. The upper path goes through a gateway endpoint to S three and DynamoDB, with no additional charge. The lower path goes through a N A T gateway to the internet, billed hourly and per gigabyte. Traffic uses a route table entry to the service prefix list. Interface endpoints, built on Private Link, bill hourly per zone plus per gigabyte, and cover most other services. A gateway endpoint only works within the same Region. Sending S three traffic through N A T adds a per-gigabyte charge for nothing. Exam tip: private servers reading S three or DynamoDB through N A T need a gateway endpoint.

1.title: Direct Connect, VPN and the Internet
1.text: Three connection options have different cost shapes. The internet charges data out per gigabyte, with no port, and suits light, occasional transfer. Site-to-Site V P N charges hourly per connection plus data out, and suits a quick, low-cost, encrypted link. Direct Connect charges port hours plus a lower data-out rate, and suits steady, high-volume transfer with consistent latency. Each V P N tunnel carries up to about one point twenty-five gigabits per second, so use several tunnels or Transit Gateway for more. Match the Direct Connect port speed to the real need. And data into A W S is free over any option. Exam tip: large, steady transfer means Direct Connect; quick or small means V P N; occasional means the internet.

1.title: Connecting VPCs: Peering, Transit Gateway and PrivateLink
1.text: Three options connect V P C s, with different costs. V P C peering has no hourly fee, though data across zones or Regions is charged, and it suits a few V P C s, point to point. Transit Gateway charges hourly per attachment plus per gigabyte processed, and suits many V P C s and sites with simpler routing. Private Link charges hourly per endpoint plus per gigabyte, and suits one service shared privately. Peering is not transitive, so a mesh grows quickly. Compare the total: attachments, processing and engineering time. Exam tip: two or three V P C s means peering is cheapest; many V P C s and on-premises sites mean Transit Gateway.

1.title: Routing to Minimize Transfer Cost
1.text: Routing choices change the bill. Keep chatty tiers in the same zone to avoid cross-zone charges, and weigh that against availability. Use private I P addresses between instances to avoid public data transfer. Use gateway endpoints for S three and DynamoDB to avoid N A T processing. Keep buckets and compute in the same Region to avoid cross-Region transfer. Put CloudFront in front of origins for cheaper egress and fewer origin reads. Compress and cache to move fewer bytes. Global Accelerator improves speed, but adds its own fee. Exam tip: cutting distance, hops and bytes beats buying more bandwidth.

1.title: CDN and Edge Caching Cost
1.text: A content delivery network can cut both latency and cost. CloudFront caches at the edge, so there are fewer origin requests. Data transfer from an A W S origin to CloudFront is not charged. CloudFront egress is usually cheaper than egress from the Region. Price classes use fewer edge locations to lower the price. A better cache hit ratio comes from longer T T L s, versioned file names and compression. Edge functions handle simple work without calling the origin. Origin Shield adds a caching layer to cut origin load. Exam tip: global users downloading large files means CloudFront cuts both latency and egress cost.

2.title: Load Balancing and DNS Cost
2.text: Load balancers and D N S have small but real costs. Load balancers bill hourly plus capacity units, so consolidate them and delete idle ones. Cross-zone balancing is always on for an Application Load Balancer, but off by default on a Network Load Balancer, where inter-zone data can be charged. Route fifty-three hosted zones carry a monthly fee per zone. Queries are charged per million, though alias queries to A W S resources are free. Latency, geolocation and failover routing add health checks, which cost money, so use only those you need. Use alias records to A W S resources instead of C name records where possible. Exam tip: an alias to an A L B or CloudFront costs nothing in queries, so prefer it.

2.title: Throttling and Bandwidth Allocation
2.text: Throttling keeps spikes from raising the bill. A P I Gateway throttling and usage plans limit requests per second and quotas per client. A W S W A F rate-based rules block floods before they reach costly back ends. S Q S buffering smooths bursts so the back end can be smaller. Lambda reserved concurrency caps how far a function can scale, and cost. For bandwidth, buy what matches the measured need. Use one V P N, and add tunnels only when throughput demands it. Right-size a Direct Connect port, and remember link aggregation can add capacity. Exam tip: when unexpected traffic spikes raise the bill, throttle at the edge, not with bigger servers.

2.title: Reviewing Existing Workloads
2.text: To review an existing workload, find the line item first. Cost Explorer by usage type shows data transfer and N A T line items. The Cost and Usage Report with Athena shows resource-level network cost. V P C Flow Logs show who talks to whom, and how much. Trusted Advisor flags idle load balancers and unused Elastic I P addresses. Cost allocation tags assign network cost by team or project. Look for cross-zone and cross-Region traffic, and for S three traffic going through N A T. Check public I P version four addresses you do not need. Budgets alert on spend, and consolidated billing pools usage across accounts. Exam tip: find the line item first, then the route that creates it.

2.title: Choosing the Cheapest Network Design
2.text: Here is the chooser. The figure branches from the traffic to the cheapest design. Private servers reaching S three or DynamoDB mean a gateway endpoint. Global downloads mean CloudFront. A steady, large hybrid transfer means Direct Connect, and a quick or small one means V P N. Many V P C s mean Transit Gateway, and a few mean peering. Internet access in a test V P C means one shared N A T gateway. Exam tip: name the traffic path, then remove the costliest hop.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Cost-Optimized Networks
2.text: Here is what the exam asks. Which N A T layout: shared, per zone or regional. Which connection: Direct Connect, V P N or the internet. Which V P C link: peering, Transit Gateway or Private Link. Which route avoids N A T, cross-zone or cross-Region charges. And which edge or throttling control reduces cost. Exam tip: look for the clues: test, steady, global, S three through N A T, many V P C s and spikes.

2.title: Design Check: Lantern and Loom Trims the Network Bill
2.text: Here is the Design Check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Three N A T gateways in a test V P C: one shared N A T gateway. S three traffic through N A T: a gateway endpoint. Overseas shoppers downloading images: CloudFront with an S three origin. A steady, large feed to the head office: Direct Connect. Four V P C s that must talk: Transit Gateway, or peering if there are few. Traffic spikes: throttling and W A F rate limits. And to find the waste: Cost Explorer usage types and Flow Logs.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Data in is free, while data out, cross-Region and cross-zone traffic are charged. For N A T, share one for test, use one per zone for production, and use gateway endpoints to avoid N A T charges. To connect, use Direct Connect for steady, large transfer, V P N for quick, peering for few V P C s and Transit Gateway for many. To reduce bytes, use CloudFront, caching, compression and throttling. And review with Cost Explorer usage types, Flow Logs and Trusted Advisor.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Private E C two instances at Lantern and Loom read terabytes from S three every day through a N A T gateway, and the N A T data processing charge is large. How can the architect reduce the cost? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: create an S three gateway endpoint and route S three traffic to it. A gateway endpoint adds no charge and keeps the traffic off the N A T gateway.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The Lantern and Loom test V P C has three subnets in three Availability Zones, each with its own N A T gateway. Test servers do not need high availability, and the team wants the lowest N A T cost. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: keep one shared N A T gateway and route all test subnets to it. That removes two hourly charges, at the cost of cross-zone traffic.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two statements about network cost are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Gateway endpoints for S three and DynamoDB add no charge, and data moving from an A W S origin to CloudFront is not charged. Inbound internet traffic is free, cross-zone traffic is charged, and Direct Connect bills port hours.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Lantern and Loom sends a large, steady data feed to its head office every day. Internet egress is costly, and the feed needs consistent latency. Which connection lowers the per-gigabyte cost and gives steady performance? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A W S Direct Connect. It bills port hours plus a lower data-out rate, with consistent latency.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Overseas shoppers download large product images from an S three bucket in one Region, and the data-out charges are high. What should the architect add to cut cost and latency? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the bucket as origin. It caches images near viewers, and transfer from S three to CloudFront is not charged.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: B and D. Question four: D. Question five: B. In Module fifteen, we bring the whole course together in a quick-reference recap and service chooser.
